newsitem.title: USA: Environmental leaders seek to protect children.
newsitem.headline: Environmental leaders seek to protect children.

text.p: International environmental officials agreed on Tuesday on steps to protect children from an unhealthy environment, including ensuring safe clean drinking water and reducing their exposure to tobacco smoke.

"Through this action the world community will work together to ensure that environmental efforts first protect the most vulnerable amongst us, our children, from the threats to health posed by pollution," U.S. Environmental Protection Agency chief Carol Browner said at the end of a two-day meeting of environmental officials from eight countries and the European Union.
In a declaration, they urged world leaders to make protecting children's enviromental health a top priority.

"We acknowledge that throughout the world, children face significant threats to health from an array of enviromental hazards. The protection of human health remains a fundamental objective of environmental policies to achieve sustainable development," it said.

It listed as among those threats contaminated drinking water, which led to four million childrens deaths annually, air pollution, including by tobacco smoke, which caused illness and death through breathing problems, and exposure to lead poisoning, which can cause low IQs and infant death.

Browner said the meeting's proposals and findings would be presented to leaders of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations at a summit in Denver in June and laid the groundwork for a U.N. special session on developments since the Rio Earth Summit in 1992.
The officials urged efforts to provide clean drinking water for all children, including helping poor countries get the technology and equipment to ensure safe water.
On improving air quality, they agreed to co-operate on education and public awareess to reduce childre's exposure to tobacco smoke.

"We affirm that environmental tobacco smoke is a significant public health risk to young children and that parents need to know about the risks of smoking in the home around their young children," the declaration said.
It also promised new efforts to reduce lead risks in gasoline, paint and drinking water.
The leaders noted that poor countries might need help from the rich in trying to ensure a better environment.
"Co-operation and partnership with the developing world is very essential," said Dutch Housing and Environmental Minister Margaretha de Boer, representing the EU presidency.
Two experts adressed the meeting on the problems of climate change. The officials said the Climate Change Treaty needed to be revised and strengthened at a conference in Kyoto, Japan, in December.

They also discussed ways to combat environmental crime such as trafficking in banned chemicals. The declaration also called for setting national enviromental protection standards and conducting risk assessments to protect children's health.
Attending the meeting were officials from the G7 countries (Canada, Britain, Japan, France, Germany, Italy and the United States), as well as Russia, the EU and the United Nations.
